item.title: [9] AlphaFold3 and Intrinsically Disordered Proteins: Reliable Monomer Prediction, Unpredictable Multimer Performance
item.description:
Score 9/10 · bioRxiv

A systematic AF3 evaluation on disordered proteins showing deterministic, seed-invariant failures in multimers and concluding that ensemble sampling is needed speaks directly to your interest in what cofolding models learn versus memorize and why they fail to sample multiple states.

Dao, T. M., Ghent, S., Uversky, V. N., Rahman, T.

AlphaFold3 represents a major advance in protein structure prediction, yet its performance on intrinsically disordered proteins remains uncharacterized. We present the first systematic evaluation of AF3 on disordered systems, revealing a striking dichotomy. For monomers, AF3's pLDDT scores reliably predict disorder (MCC: 0.693), matching AlphaFold2 and rivaling dedicated predictors. This consistency across fundamentally different architectures confirms that disorder prediction emerges from training data, not model design. For multimers, the picture grows complex. Despite comparable aggregate performance (mean DockQ: 0.563 vs 0.571), AF3 and AF2 achieve these results through fundamentally different mechanisms. Conventional structural features explain 58% of AF2's variance but only 42% of AF3's. Users cannot predict when AF3 will succeed or fail from interface properties alone. On disorder-to-order transitions (MFIB benchmark), both models perform equally well, successfully predicting final folded states. Yet seed variance analysis reveals AF3's failures are deterministic: the model converges to identical structures across independent runs, whether correct or incorrect, indicating rigid structural priors override available information. Our findings establish AF3 as reliable for the prediction of monomer disorder but unpredictable for multimers. Architectural innovation alone cannot overcome training data bias. Progress demands disorder-enriched datasets and ensemble sampling, not merely novel architectures.

item.title: [7] Pre-catalytic activation pathway of the Smc5/6 complex
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Cryo-EM heterogeneity analysis resolving Smc5/6 as a conformational ensemble with a continuous Cross-to-Juxtaposed transition, plus network modeling of the pathway, is a good real-data example of the kind of ensembles your steering work aims to reproduce.

Wong, J. S. K., Loke, M. S., Pradhan, B., Kanno, T. et al.

The Smc5/6 complex (Smc5/6) preserves genome stability through ATP-dependent DNA organization, but the structural details that prime the complex for productive DNA engagement remain unknown. Here, we combine cryo-electron microscopy and conformational heterogeneity analysis to define the pre-catalytic activation pathway of Smc5/6. We show that in the absence of ATP and DNA, Smc5/6 exists as a heterogeneous conformational ensemble composed predominantly of two conformations termed Bridge and Cross. In the presence of DNA alone, Smc5/6 adopts a Juxtaposed conformation that brings the ATPase heads into proximity, aligning them for nucleotide engagement. With both ATP and DNA associated, Smc5/6 establishes an Engaged architecture, within which DNA stabilizes its head-associated binding cavity through local remodeling of the complex. Conformational heterogeneity analyses suggest a continuous structural transition between the Cross and Juxtaposed states, while anisotropic network modeling identifies the Bridge-Cross-Juxtaposed-Engaged sequence as the mechanically favored pathway connecting the four experimentally observed conformations. Together, these findings support a pre-catalytic conformational pathway for Smc5/6 activation and provide a structural framework for understanding how conformational heterogeneity gives rise to an activation-competent motor state.

item.title: [8] Inference-Time Steering Across Scaffolds and Epitopes for Sample-Efficient De Novo Nanobody Design
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Feynman-Kac and SMC inference-time steering for de novo nanobody design, with dynamic compute allocation across conditioning configurations, is a close cousin of the inference-time steering you build and transfers to allocating budget across conditions.

Mason Minot, Simon Friedensohn, C\'edric R. Weber

arXiv:2610.13844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative molecular design typically relies on over-generation and post-hoc filtering. Inference-time steering methods like Feynman-Kac (FK) steering improve efficiency by biasing trajectories toward high-reward candidates, yet they optimize within a single fixed configuration. In de novo nanobody design, upfront commitment to conditioning choices like scaffold identity or target epitope creates a bottleneck. Since yield varies across these conditions, steering unpromising setups wastes compute. We recast generative condition selection as an inference-time resource-allocation problem. We propose two dynamic budget allocators: a joint Global Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) formulation that steers and allocates compute across configurations concurrently, and a decoupled approach adapting Batched Successive Elimination (BaSE). Empirically, these dynamic allocators increase the yield of designable candidates per GPU-hour nearly 5$\times$ without sacrificing diversity across distinct therapeutic targets and generative configurations.

item.title: [8] Spanning Diffusion and Flow-based Posterior Sampling via Exact Gaussian Conditioning
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

β-Flow unifies flow, diffusion and decorrelated priors for inverse problems through an exact Kalman-style Gaussian conditioning step that needs no network gradients and clarifies the implicit assumptions of existing guided samplers, which bears directly on steering with experimental observations.

Teo Deveney, Lea Bogensperger, Hok Shing Wong

arXiv:2610.13812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flow-matching and diffusion models are increasingly used as priors for linear inverse problems, however, most methods are bespoke to one class of trajectory prior. Plug-and-play methods have been proposed, however these implicitly decorrelate the guided trajectory, resulting in broad priors that can struggle when data is sparse. This work proposes $\beta$-Flow: a general plug-and-play method indexed by a correlation parameter $\beta$ that generalises over flow, diffusion, and decorrelated priors, and a confidence parameter $\kappa$ that controls how strongly the path distribution is enforced. Each step requires only one forward evaluation of a denoising network, followed by a Gaussian conditioning step. This step is an exact Kalman update that is not dependent on network gradients. We show that many existing guided samplers can be interpreted as instances or approximations of our method, each implicitly using a different trajectory prior and operator in place of the Kalman gain. From this viewpoint, we provide a qualitative comparison of methods in terms of their implicit biases and assumptions. We demonstrate consistently state-of-the-art level performance across 7 inverse problems over 4 datasets in terms of PSNR and SSIM. Moreover, we demonstrate the utility of this prior control, by showing that confident high correlations (strict priors) work best when observations are less informative, while low correlation is preferred when observations are more informative, reflecting the complementary roles of the prior and likelihood in Bayesian inference.

item.title: [8] The CAHRA Challenge: A Community-Wide Assessment of Cryo-EM Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

Zhong-lab-led community benchmark with ground-truth datasets for cryo-EM compositional and continuous heterogeneity, giving you an evaluation standard for the heterogeneity methods your ensemble work is measured against.

Feathers, J. R., Heeter, R., Woollard, G., Hanson, S. M. et al.

The ability of cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to interrogate the atomic structure and motion of biomolecules has motivated the development of a wide range of algorithms for heterogeneity analysis. However, evaluating and comparing these methods remains challenging because ground-truth structures are generally unknown for experimental samples. Here, we introduce the 2026 Community-Wide Assessment of Heterogeneous Reconstruction Algorithms (CAHRA), a community-wide challenge centered on three benchmark datasets that probe distinct tasks in heterogeneity analysis. These include (1) compositional heterogeneity arising from mixtures of distinct protein complexes, (2) continuous conformational variability and atomic modeling, and (3) entanglement between molecular conformation and particle pose. We describe the design, construction, and validation of these datasets, as well as their use in the recently completed CAHRA Challenge.

item.title: [7] Looking Under the Streetlight: Evaluation in Generative Molecular Dynamics
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

A position paper by Olsson, Noé, Rotskoff and Lindorff-Larsen arguing that generative MD evaluation lets models match reported proxies while being wrong on the claimed ensemble properties, directly relevant to how you validate BioEmu-style ensemble emulators.

Simon Olsson, Frank No\'e, Grant M. Rotskoff, Kresten Lindorff-Larsen

arXiv:2610.12518v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This position paper argues that the generative molecular dynamics (GenMD) community is not properly evaluating its progress: current evaluations let a model match what is reported while being arbitrarily wrong on what was claimed, which risks over-claiming advantage over classical baselines. This reflects a structural misalignment between common evaluation practices and the scientific tasks the field sets for itself. The reason is that the ground truth---exhaustive molecular dynamics on the systems of interest---is computationally costly, and this cost is what motivates the field. With ground truth inaccessible, evaluation drifts toward convenient proxies, and the resulting norms entrench easily. We identify misaligned evaluation patterns that persist as a community-level equilibrium, and propose concrete observables, reporting standards, and benchmark designs, both computational and experimental, that better reflect what GenMD aspires to deliver. Our aim is to give the field shared language and tools for evaluation that match its scientific ambitions before today's conventions calcify into norms.

item.title: [7] Opening the Black Box of Classifier-Free Guidance via Information Bottleneck
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

An information-theoretic account of when classifier-free guidance matters during sampling, with a training-free adaptive activation rule that could directly inform guidance schedules in your steering platform.

Jiayang Gao, Tianyi Zheng, Jiayang Zou, Fengxiang Yang, Luyao Fan, Lv Tang, Bo Li, Jia Wang

arXiv:2610.13369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard technique for improving conditional generation in diffusion models, yet its activation schedule is usually selected heuristically. In practice, most existing CFG-based methods rely on a pre-defined activation policy throughout inference, while recent dynamic variants often depend on hand-designed schedules without a principled theoretical explanation of when conditional information is most useful. In order to understand how the informational relevance between conditioning inputs and the score function evolves over the course of generation, we explore when guidance should be activated from an information-theoretic perspective. In this work, we formulate the diffusion trajectory as a time-dependent information bottleneck and show that the effectiveness of conditional information is not uniform throughout sampling, but becomes significantly stronger after a critical stage characterized by a Fisher-information balance condition. Motivated by this insight, we propose a training-free dynamic CFG strategy for inference. Rather than prescribing a fixed schedule in advance, our method constructs a stochastic process from conditional and unconditional score statistics and activates guidance when the estimated guidance gain crosses a prescribed threshold. This yields an adaptive activation rule that aligns condition injection with the underlying generation dynamics, while also recovering interval-based guidance as a limiting special case. Extensive experiments across diverse architectures and tasks, demonstrate that our method is effective, robust, and broadly applicable. Beyond empirical improvements, our framework provides an interpretation of dynamic guidance methods and a principled foundation for inference-time control in conditional diffusion models.

item.title: [7] Some remarks on the connection between generative diffusion and optimal transport
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Biroli and Mézard tie diffusion and flow-matching generation to entropic optimal transport and the speciation transition, a theory exposition that sharpens intuition for how diffusion samplers behave.

Giulio Biroli, Marc M\'ezard

arXiv:2610.13614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We discuss three simple connections between generative diffusion and optimal transport. First, the joint law of the data and of their Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noising is, at every time, the solution of an entropic optimal-transport problem, at a temperature set by the noise level. Backward diffusion can consequently be read as an annealing which gradually decreases the entropic regularization. Second, we study the speciation transition--how the modes of the data distribution emerge during generation--and compare how it happens in diffusion and flow matching with respect to optimal transport. Using Gaussian mixtures as high-dimensional example, we show that the dynamical instability through which diffusion and flow matching separate the modes becomes, for optimal transport, an exponentially thin boundary layer at the beginning of generation, which is rounded by entropic regularization. Third, considering a generic forward dynamics with a general confining potential, we show that the backward process driven by the score also satisfies a drift-based variational principle whose minimal cost is the entropy difference between initial and final distributions.

item.title: [7] Sequence context decodes multi-state conformational heterogeneity from crystallographic B-factors
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Recovering residue-wise multi-state heterogeneity from crystallographic B-factors with a sequence-aware model speaks directly to extracting ensemble information from crystallographic data and could serve as a prior for your refinement work.

Wang, Y., Cai, M., Ma, Y., Shi, T. et al.

Protein function is governed by conformational ensembles, yet the overwhelming majority of experimentally determined structures capture only static snapshots, leaving the multi-state heterogeneity that underlies biological activity largely inaccessible. X-ray crystallography, the dominant source of these structures, does carry one experimental proxy for motion, the atomic B-factor, but crystal packing and refinement artifacts frequently obscure its link to solution-state dynamics. Here we show that sequence context is sufficient to decode a protein's multi-state conformational heterogeneity from this seemingly noisy signal. We introduce the B-Factor Corrector (BFC), a fine-tuned protein language model that reframes B-factor analysis from a purely physical calculation into a sequence-context-aware translation task. By leveraging deep contextual embeddings to decouple intrinsic conformational heterogeneity from lattice constraints, BFC recovers the residue-wise heterogeneity ranking derived from crystallographic structural ensembles, reproducing the normalized profile at a Pearson correlation of 0.83 while correcting the distortions that analytical formulas leave in the raw signal. We further demonstrate the utility of this sequence-inferred signal across structural-biology applications: it provides an integrable prior for molecular docking that is statistically equivalent to experimental B-factors, unmasks cryptic conformational heterogeneity essential for chaperone function, and guides the energetic refinement of antibody interfaces to resolve steric conflicts. These results suggest that the static structures of the Protein Data Bank can be effectively repurposed to decode the conformational heterogeneity latent within them.

item.title: [7] Autonomous AI agents discover reverse transcriptases with tandem repeat arrays
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Claude Code agents autonomously mining 1.9 billion protein clusters and surfacing a new reverse transcriptase family is a concrete, serious example of agents doing computational biology discovery, plus the striking tandem-repeat RT biology.

Yoon, P. H., Athukoralage, J. S., Ameisen, E., Kauderer-Abrams, E. et al.

Metagenomic databases hold vast quantities of unexplored genetic material that can seed tools for biotechnology and medicine, but discovery is limited by our ability to examine sequence data at scale. Here, we show that large language models (LLMs) in an autonomous harness can alleviate this bottleneck and surface novel molecular systems. We deployed Claude Code instances to survey reverse transcriptase (RT) loci across 1.9 billion protein clusters. Among the top candidates were array-associated RTs (ART), a novel family of jumbo-phage RTs coupled with an array of ~200-nucleotide units and a dedicated partner gene. Session transcripts show that Claude identified the ART family by directly examining its DNA sequences and recognizing the atypical repeats, a behavior attributable to specific Mythos 5 internal signals that respond to repeated DNA. ART arrays are highly expressed and appear as discrete units during Staphylococcus phage infection, suggesting an RT system directed by a repertoire of distinct RNAs. These findings indicate that LLMs can autonomously detect anomalies and drive analyses to initiate biological discoveries.

item.title: [7] Ab initio CryoEM maps minimizing preferred orientation problems in heterogeneous mixtures: ReconSIREN
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

ReconSIREN is an ab initio neural cryo-EM reconstruction method that handles preferred orientation and outputs a conformational landscape, which is directly relevant to heterogeneity modeling, though it is a method variant rather than a conceptual advance.

Herreros, D., Sorzano, C. O. S., Carazo, J. M.

Cryo-Electron Microscopy (CryoEM) Single Particle Analysis (SPA) is pivotal for elucidating protein structures and their conformational dynamics. Several critical steps are required to obtain accurate maps. First, the \textit{ab initio} relative orientations and shifts between images must be determined. Second, the common issue of specimens presenting a preferred orientation should be adequately addressed. Third, all of the above must account for particle flexibility and sample heterogeneity. Additionally, these steps are interrelated, making the search for all these parameters a real challenge when considering convergence robustness. In this context, we present ReconSIREN, a novel deep learning framework that addresses the key steps outlined before in an \textit{ab initio} manner while greatly minimizing one of the most important practical burdens in SPA, namely the errors introduced in the CryoEM maps by the existence of preferred orientations; the latter is achieved by a change of the optimization approach that avoids the so-called ``attraction problem'', and by the introduction of a new type of geometrical priors. It does so fully \textit{ab initio}, using deep learning training/inference steps without resorting to more traditional optimization approaches, and generating highly accurate initial reconstructions. We present maps as both homogeneous (consensus) maps and a full conformational landscape for analyzing flexibility and heterogeneity. Thanks to its Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, ReconSIREN distributes the estimation workload across independent experts, improving optimization efficiency and simplifying the process.

item.title: [9] RNA catalysis emerges from dynamic structural ensembles
item.description:
Score 9/10 · Nature

Cryo-EM heterogeneity analysis resolving 76 coexisting RNase P RNA conformers and linking Mg2+ dynamics to catalysis is a ready-made ensemble-versus-single-structure test case for your steering and ensemble-refinement work, and you would be surprised to have missed it.

Maximilia F. S. Degenhardt, Hermann F. Degenhardt, Bapurao A. Bhoge, Yun-Tzai Lee et al.

The dynamic interplay between RNA structure and its associated Mg2+ ions is central to RNA function yet remains poorly understood at a near-atomic level1-4. Here, using a heterogeneity-focused protocol for cryo-electron microscopy data analysis of conformationally flexible RNA particles, we determined the structures of RNase P RNA ensembles composed of 76 coexisting active and inactive conformers that differ in a transient tertiary interaction that is critical for activity. The binding of the accessory protein does not change the local structure but induces thermodynamic allostery that enhances catalysis by altering the dynamics of the tertiary interaction. Four distinct classes of Mg2+ ions have critical roles in the structure, dynamics and catalysis of the conformational ensembles. Together, these findings establish a new paradigm in which catalysis is regulated through multimodal communications coupled with the dynamics of RNA-Mg2+ conformational ensembles, rather than a single static catalytic structure in a single action mode.

item.title: [9] Bayesian Sampling of Structural Ensembles: The Role of Ensemble-Counting Measures
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

Shows that Bayesian sampling of maximum-entropy ensemble refinement against experimental data needs an explicit ensemble-counting measure and proposes the Jeffreys measure, directly relevant to posterior sampling of conformational ensembles with experimental restraints.

Ivan Gilardoni, Giovanni Bussi

arXiv:2606.18495v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Structural ensemble refinement is widely used to integrate molecular simulations with experimental measurements. While most applications focus on the maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) ensemble, Bayesian sampling of the posterior distribution can provide uncertainty estimates and posterior averages for arbitrary observables. A notable step in this direction was introduced by the Bayesian Energy Landscape Tilting (BELT) framework, where sampling is performed on a family of maximum-entropy ensembles parametrized by Lagrange multipliers. Here, we show that Bayesian sampling in this setting requires an explicit choice of ensemble-counting measure. In particular, the flat measure in Lagrange-multiplier space used in the original BELT formulation leads to a posterior distribution that is formally non-normalizable for finite reference trajectories. We propose the Jeffreys measure as an invariant ensemble-counting prescription, restoring normalizability in the finite-sample situations considered here, and providing a consistent definition of posterior averages. Using both an analytically tractable Gaussian model and maximum-entropy refinement of RNA oligomer simulations, we compare different ensemble-counting measures and show that they can significantly affect Bayesian estimates. The resulting methodology has been implemented in the \texttt{MDRefine} software package.
